item.title: 莫斯科附近的一座仓库着火。乌克兰无人机机组人员准备再次发动袭击
item.description:
夜间，一波又一波的乌克兰无人机袭击了莫斯科郊外的大型物流中心。第二天早上，俄罗斯最大的零售仓库之一仍然熊熊燃烧，黑烟升腾到天空。
数百英里外，乌克兰无人机机组人员在完成一晚的工作后几乎没有停下来，就开始准备另一次袭击。
一小群士兵迅速集结在乌克兰南部的一片向日葵田里，聚集了大约 20 架装有炸药的小型飞机无人机，然后将它们发射到俄罗斯。
美联社记者团队观察了周日上午乌克兰第 413“突袭”无人系统团的发射——这是对乌克兰战争努力迅速扩大的一部分的罕见观察。
这是乌克兰的最新策略——远程无人机旨在将战争深入俄罗斯境内，攻击远离前线的军事、工业和后勤场所。
基辅今年加大了对俄罗斯的攻击力度，使用远程导弹和大量无人机瞄准军事工业和能源设施。它还对巨型Wildberry 仓库进行了越来越多的打击，烧毁了这家俄罗斯在线零售巨头价值数十亿美元的商品。
在莫斯科全面入侵乌克兰近 4.5 年后，这些袭击让俄罗斯公众重新认识了这场战争。袭击的规模还迫使俄罗斯军方将防空范围扩展到更大的地区，扰乱了机场，引发了燃料短缺，并削弱了俄罗斯的士气。
该团指挥官叶夫亨·卡拉斯 (Yevhen Karas) 表示，他的部队还在几个小时前参与了对莫斯科以南约 45 公里（28 英里）处的野莓仓库的袭击，这是乌克兰迄今为止对俄罗斯最大规模的袭击之一。
卡拉斯说，“如果我们想要获得稳定、长期的和平，以及正常的和平”，乌克兰就需要惩罚克里姆林宫。
他补充说，“他们的伤亡越大”，他们就会越早寻求和平。
基辅官员的目标是让俄罗斯公众感受到战争的后果，并向俄罗斯总统弗拉基米尔·普京施压，要求其谈判和平解决方案。到目前为止，普京还没有表现出他打算结束战争的迹象。
然而，卡拉斯认为，乌克兰的远程打击行动对俄罗斯经济的影响正在让俄罗斯普通民众认识到战争的代价，并希望这将促使莫斯科在美国斡旋的双方谈判陷入僵局数月后重返谈判桌。
周日早上，在无人机升空之前，卡拉斯拿出一支黑色记号笔，在机身上写下一条信息：“莫斯科在天空下燃烧，红色火焰升得如此温暖和高高，黑烟在城镇上空移动，火光照亮了周围的夜晚。”
与大多数乌克兰现役军人一样，卡拉斯在 2022 年 2 月 24 日俄罗斯入侵乌克兰之前过着截然不同的生活。
但那天，38岁的大学主修哲学的他和他的兄弟弗拉基米尔双双志愿奔赴前线。他的兄弟在保卫基辅地区时被杀。在接下来的几个月里，卡拉斯晋升为乌克兰特种作战部队的一名军官。
2024 年，卡拉斯被任命为新组建的第 413 突袭无人系统团的指挥官，该团最初是一支使用无人机执行侦察和其他战场任务的部队。
随着无人机技术的发展和飞行距离从数百英里增加到一千多英里，他的部队的任务是使用乌克兰国产 FP-1 无人机对俄罗斯深处的目标进行远程行动。
该部门的其他成员包括一名前歌剧歌手、一名电脑程序员、一名说唱歌手和一名大提琴手。他们的日常工作现在集中在一系列非常简单的任务上：准备无人机、检查系统、将其移动到位并发射。
该部队的奖章——世界各地的军队称之为“挑战硬币”——一侧带有部队的徽章，是一支风格化的三爪箭头。另一幅是克里姆林宫在火焰中的浮雕，一架无人机飞过其上空。
卡拉斯表示，在战争的现阶段，莫斯科应该敬畏天空。
卡拉斯说：“莫斯科人应该在他们美妙的地铁里过夜，就像基辅居民多年来一直在地下躲避俄罗斯导弹和无人机袭击一样。”
回到向日葵田，无人机升空后，士兵们就收拾好装备开走了，几乎没有留下任何活动痕迹。

item.title: 哈里王子和梅根将带着孩子返回英国
item.description:
伦敦（美联社）——美联社周三获悉，哈里王子和他的妻子梅根已决定从今年秋天开始返回英国进行长期逗留，但他们不会恢复作为王室工作成员的角色。
据一位与苏塞克斯夫妇关系密切的人士透露，这对夫妇的孩子，7 岁的阿奇王子和 5 岁的莉莉贝特公主，已经在英国学校就读，并将于 9 月开始上课。这家人计划住在伦敦郊外的一处私人非皇家住宅，但计划保留他们在加利福尼亚州蒙特西托的住宅以及在葡萄牙的度假房产。
《每日电讯报》最先报道了这一事件。周三晚上，当被要求在华盛顿与美国退伍军人举行的圆桌会议上讨论美联社的报道时，哈里回答说：“没什么可说的。”
六年多前，哈里和梅根放弃了王室职责，搬到加利福尼亚州，通过与 Netflix 和 Spotify 签订利润丰厚的合同谋生。尽管从那时起，哈里与王室其他成员的关系恶化，但哈利最近表示有和解的兴趣，这样他就可以花更多时间与父亲查尔斯三世国王在一起，后者正在接受一种未公开的癌症治疗。
查尔斯于周日得知了这对夫妇的计划。哈里和梅根上个月访问了英国。
白金汉宫有一项政策，不对有关王室非工作成员的猜测发表评论。哈里和梅根的代表拒绝置评。
据一位与苏塞克斯夫妇关系密切的消息人士透露，梅根将继续在英国领导她的 As Ever 公司，而哈里则可以花更多时间与他位于英国的慈善机构合作。
自从哈里和梅根搬到南加州蒙特西托的一栋豪宅后，他们与王室的关系就一直很紧张。
在一系列采访和哈里的回忆录《备用》中，这对夫妇表示，他们离开英国是为了逃避王室生活的限制，并批评王室官员对梅根的心理健康不敏感，同时声称至少一名王室成员在她怀第一个孩子时表达了种族主义观点。梅根形容自己是混血儿。
哈利与英国小报的长期法律斗争加剧了这些紧张局势，他声称这些小报在他年轻时非法侵入了他的手机并侵犯了他的隐私。王子在一系列针对媒体的诉讼中败诉，其中包括针对《每日邮报》出版商的诉讼，该诉讼已于上个月结束。
在法院裁定哈利和该案的其他原告应对出版商的法律费用负责后，最新的审判使哈利面临着数百万英镑的潜在账单。美联社提交的文件显示，其法律费用达 3450 万英镑（4700 万美元）。
哈里还卷入了与英国政府的法律纠纷，此前政府委员会拒绝授权警方为王子及其家人在英国提供保护。王子表示，他和他的家人需要武装警察的保护，因为他们仅仅因为是王室成员而面临危险，无论他们是否是在职王室成员。
去年因安全问题在法庭上败诉后，哈里表示希望与家人重建关系。
哈里告诉英国广播公司：“我很想与家人和解。继续争吵已经没有意义了。”“我不知道我父亲还能活多久。”
上个月，哈里回到英国参加一系列慈善活动。梅根和孩子们参加了哈里王子的部分访问，并在国王位于英格兰西部的海格罗夫庄园与国王共度了时光。这是自 2022 年已故女王伊丽莎白二世登基五十周年以来，阿奇和莉莉贝特第一次见到祖父。
虽然哈里最近会见了他的父亲，但与他的兄弟、王位继承人威廉王子的关系没有任何升温的迹象。
英国广播公司 (BBC) 前王室记者彼得·亨特 (Peter Hunt) 表示，这一意外消息将使威廉“勃然大怒”。
“短期内，哈里将能够加深与父亲的和解，”亨特告诉英国新闻协会。“而他回到家乡将使他的兄弟更难回避和解。”

item.title: 卡米拉女王希望她能在访问癌症慈善机构时分享国王的诊断结果
item.description:
伦敦（美联社）——英国女王卡米拉表示，她在丈夫的癌症诊断结果公开宣布前几天就知道了，并发现在那段时间访问癌症中心时很难不谈论他的病情。
国王查理三世于 2024 年 2 月 5 日宣布，他正在接受一种未公开的癌症治疗，这打破了王室将健康问题保密的传统。国王公开谈论他的诊断结果被认为说服了更多的男性接受前列腺癌和其他形式的疾病检查。
女王表示，在宣布查尔斯的诊断结果一周前，她在伦敦皇家自由医院开设了玛吉癌症支持中心，当时她“渴望”谈论查尔斯的诊断，但她知道自己不能。卡米拉自 2008 年起担任 Maggie’s 总裁，该公司在英国 27 家医院运营癌症中心。
“当时没有人能说什么。那是相当困难的，”卡米拉在周三发布的纪念该慈善机构成立 30 周年的视频中说道。“我几乎要说什么，但你知道，我觉得现在还不是说的时候。”
最近有关国王的最新消息称，随着他继续接受癌症治疗，他的健康状况正在朝着积极的方向发展。
卡米拉的八分钟视频是根据女王和玛吉首席执行官劳拉·李之间的对话改编的，劳拉·李表示，自从国王宣布确诊以来，参观该慈善机构中心的男性人数增加了 12%。
玛吉提供信息、咨询和其他形式的支持，帮助癌症患者克服恐惧，在接受治疗的同时继续生活。
卡米拉说，在查尔斯确诊后，她更好地理解了对此类服务的需求。
“看看我的丈夫，没有什么能阻止他，”她说。“他只是说，‘这是我的方式。我会应对它。’”

item.title: 卡梅洛·安东尼寻求新审判，法官不再参与德克萨斯州田径比赛杀人案
item.description:
得克萨斯州麦金尼（美联社）——星期三，在一场重要听证会之前，主审德克萨斯州少年卡梅洛·安东尼谋杀案的法官被撤回此案，听证会决定是否对一名 17 岁运动员在高中田径比赛中被刺死的事件进行新的审判。
对于现年 19 岁的安东尼来说，免职是一次法律上的胜利，他的律师希望法官在 6 月份的审判后停止审理此案，部分原因是法官在一次电视采访中表示，陪审员在对奥斯汀·梅特卡夫被杀一案做出有罪判决时“做得对”。
这张由德克萨斯州刑事司法部于 2026 年 8 月 18 日星期二提供的预订照片显示的是卡梅洛·安东尼。（德克萨斯州刑事司法部，美联社）
被判处 35 年监禁的安东尼在达拉斯郊区的法庭上，当一名来访法官下令州地方法官约翰·罗奇回避时，他穿着绿色的监狱连身裤。法官迈克尔·奇蒂后来被指派审理此案。
麦金尼法庭外，走廊里爆发出欢呼声，一些安东尼的支持者高呼“释放卡梅洛！”在停车场。
安东尼的律师在一份声明中表示：“今天的裁决回答了一个基本问题：一个理性、充分知情的观察者是否会看到罗奇法官的行为，并相信他可以公平、公正地考虑重新审判的动议。”
周四，安东尼预计将返回法庭参加听证会，以确定是否需要重审。
今年夏天，陪审员驳回了安东尼去年在体育场露天看台与梅特卡夫对峙时出于自卫的主张。安东尼在审判期间没有出庭作证。其他出庭的学生描述了安东尼在春雨中拒绝离开梅特卡夫团队的帐篷引发的激烈争执。
该案引起了全国关注，部分原因是大量社交媒体帖子以种族术语放大了这起杀戮事件。安东尼是黑人；梅特卡夫是白人。然而，双方律师都告诉陪审员，这场悲剧与种族无关。
安东尼的法律团队辩称，需要重审，部分原因是罗奇执行了严格的法庭规则，他们称这些规则限制了公众参与诉讼程序。他们周三还关注了罗奇在审判结束后向达拉斯一家电视台发表的评论。
在听证会开始时播放的采访中，罗奇被问及陪审团是否“正确”。
“是的，他们做到了，”罗奇说，并补充道：“无论他们说什么，他们都是对的。”
2026 年 8 月 19 日星期三，科林县法院位于德克萨斯州麦金尼。（Elías Valverde II/《达拉斯晨报》，美联社）
2026 年 8 月 19 日星期三，德克萨斯州麦金尼，法官小约翰·罗奇 (John Roach Jr.) 被回避参加安东尼谋杀案下一阶段的审判，卡梅洛·安东尼 (Karmelo Anthony) 的支持者在科林县法院外庆祝。（Elías Valverde II/《达拉斯晨报》，美联社）
在采访中，罗奇还为自己的法庭规则进行了辩护，并谈到了有关此案的网上帖子的冲击。
来访的法官西德·哈勒表示，他不认识罗奇，他相信罗奇在重审听证会上会是公平的，但考虑到其他人可能会觉得这件事，他同意辩方回避的请求。哈尔在书面命令中表示，证据表明法官的“公正性可能会受到合理质疑”，并命令另一名法官“主持所有进一步的诉讼程序”。
裁决后，罗奇没有立即回应置评请求。
检察官比尔·维尔斯基敦促法庭保留罗奇。他说法官“没有做错任何事”，他的法庭规则是为了保护审判的公正性，这导致示威者离开法院。裁决后，威尔斯基没有立即回应置评请求。
去年，随着全国对这起杀戮事件的关注加剧，梅特卡夫和安东尼的家人表示，他们一直是骚扰的目标。
“我们都收到了死亡威胁，”威尔斯基说。
当安东尼坐在纪念高中看台上的帐篷下时，几所学校正在比赛。目击者作证称，梅特卡夫和其他人多次要求安东尼离开，导致冲突升级。
检察官称安东尼挑衅了梅特卡夫，目击者作证称安东尼是侵略者。
据警方报告称，安东尼有一次把手伸进一个袋子里，回答道：“摸摸我，看看会发生什么。”
据目击者称，梅特卡夫推了安东尼，安东尼随后拔出一把刀刺伤了他的胸部。
美联社撰稿人吉姆·韦尔图诺对奥斯汀的这篇报道做出了贡献。

item.title: 受邀媒体和军事人员在加州太空军基地被枪指着
item.description:
加利福尼亚州范登堡太空部队基地（美联社）——据当地新闻报道，应邀参加加利福尼亚州范登堡太空部队基地活动的五名新闻记者和两名军人被安全人员持枪短暂拘留，他们认为他们是闯入者。
这起事件发生在周一，当时正值加利福尼亚州圣巴巴拉附近的联邦机场为导弹操作员新训练设施举行破土动工仪式，该设施仅限受邀者参加。Noozhawk 和 KEYT 的记者均被拘留，两家媒体都发表了详细介绍拘留情况的文章。
在给 Noozhawk 的一份声明中，太空发射 Delta 30 公共事务发言人称这一事件是沟通中断。
声明称：“范登堡太空部队基地的未经授权进入尝试的数量正在增加。”“每一个潜在的未经授权的存在都必须被视为合法威胁，除非有其他证明。虽然我们认识到这可能令人不安，但基地及其人员的安全是我们的首要任务。”
据新闻报道，记者和军人是由穿着制服的公共事务工作人员乘坐政府小型货车护送到基地的车队的一部分，突然被命令下车并举起双手。
据基特报道，警察用枪指着，拉响了警报，大门入口处设置了路障。
据努兹霍克报道，分配到该基地的两名军事人员——一名是士兵，一名是下级军官——被戴上手铐并安置在基地车辆中，而平民则被命令坐在路边。
KSBY-TV 和 Santa Maria Times/Lompoc Record 等媒体的记者被扣留了 30 多分钟，导致他们错过了活动。所有人都被释放，没有发生进一步的事件。
“我们尊重军方为基地提供安全保障的需要，”Noozhawk 的主编汤姆·博尔顿 (Tom Bolton) 在周三的一份声明中表示。“但显然发生的事情是不幸的、不必要的，而且有潜在的危险，因为有人拔出了枪。”
博尔顿表示，他希望在本周晚些时候与基地领导层进行对话，回顾所发生的事情，以防止未来再次发生类似情况。

item.title: 心理学家证明林赛·克兰西对杀害她的三个孩子不负刑事责任
item.description:
马萨诸塞州普利茅斯（美联社）——周三在另一起谋杀案审判中，一名为辩方作证的心理学家表示，林赛·克兰西并不理解因心理健康问题而杀害三个孩子的“错误”。
保罗·蔡泽尔的证词是迄今为止最有力的证据，支持辩方的论点，即克兰西不应承担谋杀的法律责任，因为她患有双相情感障碍，并且在试图自杀之前杀死了她的三个孩子时，她患有一种罕见的精神疾病，称为产后精神病。克兰西死后，蔡泽尔开始在医院看望病人。
蔡泽尔说：“她无法使自己的行为符合法治。她对自己行为的错误没有认识到。”她补充说，她患有“精神疾病或缺陷”。
编者注：这个故事包括对自杀的讨论。如果您或您认识的人需要帮助，请拨打 988 或发短信联系美国的全国自杀和危机生命热线。
36 岁的克兰西对谋杀卡兰、道森和科拉·克兰西的指控不认罪，三人年龄从 8 个月到 5 岁不等。产后精神病与分娩后的压力、睡眠不足和荷尔蒙变化有关。研究人员估计，这种情况比产后抑郁症更严重且不太常见，每 1000 名女性中就有 1 到 2 人在产后遭受这种情况的困扰。
检察官称，这位前分娩护士策划了 2023 年 1 月的杀戮，并派她的丈夫去给他们的一个孩子拿药和为家人买晚餐，设法让他离开家。
蔡泽尔说，他与克兰西一起度过了超过 35 个小时的时间，进行了数十次探访，并查看了她的病历。他说，她于 2022 年 12 月去了围产期诊所，因为她觉得自己“大脑受损”，“她应该自杀”，而且“永远不会好转”。她还表现出精神错乱的迹象，很偏执，担心人们会听到她的想法，担心她会失去孩子。
“她担心她的孩子会离开她，她再也见不到他们了，”他说。
蔡泽尔说，但仅仅因为她处于精神病状态，并不意味着她不能做“日常生活任务”，比如开车和上网搜索，指的是案发当天她带女儿去看医生，和孩子们在雪地里玩耍，并在网上搜索药店和餐馆。
“所以事实上，她没有谈论角落里的独角兽，她没有含糊其词，她也没有无法行走，根据你的观点，在一定程度上的医学确定性，这是否意味着她没有处于精神病状态？”克兰西的律师凯文·雷丁顿问道。
在盘问中，检察官指出了蔡泽尔在有关克兰西的报告中所犯的错误，并质疑他在将克兰西视为病人并与辩方合作（包括与雷丁顿一起出席新闻发布会）时是否能够客观地对待她的诊断。
蔡泽尔承认，克兰西的医疗记录中没有任何内容表明她听到有人要求她自杀，只是她告诉她的护理人员“她想死”。
检察官质疑克兰西自杀未遂的严重性。勒死孩子后，克兰西从二楼的窗户跳下，腰部以下仍然瘫痪。
检察官沙南·白金汉还阅读了克兰西所在的州立精神病院图克斯伯里医院的每日报告，其中包括杀戮周年纪念日以及她孩子们的生日。这些报道提到她的父母有时会来看望她或她与其他患者交谈。但他们从未提及她为纪念孩子们所做的任何事情。
雷丁顿问蔡泽尔，他是否在医院的记录中看到了她在医院期间“欢笑、聚会和度过愉快时光”的任何内容。
“林赛·克兰西有糟糕的日子，也有更糟糕的日子，”蔡泽尔说。
蔡泽尔还表示，克兰西经常谈论她的孩子，目的是消除检察官关于她从未提及过他们的论点。“她真的很爱他们，想念他们，每天、几乎每时每刻都在想念他们，”蔡泽尔说。
如果谋杀罪名成立，克兰西将面临终身监禁且不得假释。如果因缺乏刑事责任而被判无罪，她将被送往州立精神卫生机构。

item.title: 检察官表示，科米的贝壳帖子可能被解读为特朗普的威胁，“没有严重争议”
item.description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Justice is defending itsprosecution of former FBI Director James Comey, saying “there is no serious dispute” that a social media post of seashells he made last year could be understood as a threat againstPresident Donald Trump.
Prosecutors also called into question Comey’s account that he had found the seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47” while walking on a beach in North Carolina and suggested that his May 2025 post on Instagram was an effort to generate attention for a forthcoming novel about a social media personality whose words inspire his fans to attack his foes.
The arguments in motionslate Tuesday represent the government’s most detailed explanation of its indictment and were filed in response towide-ranging defense efforts to dismiss the caseon grounds including that it constitutes a vindictive prosecution and that Comey’s post did not amount to a true threat. Comey’s lawyers contend that investigators in the case misled judges, submitted documents containing false statements, withheld key facts and repeatedly came up empty in their efforts to prove that Comey intended a physical threat or knew that the number 86 could suggest violence.
The U.S. Department of Justice logo is seen on a podium before a news conference, May 4, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)
The entry for “86”from Merriam-Webster, the dictionary used by The Associated Press, says its meaning is “to throw out,” “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to.” Trump, a Republican, is the 47th president.
Federal prosecutors maintain that the photo of the seashells, which Comey said he found on the beach, constituted a threat against Trump. Comey deleted the post shortly after he put it up, saying he did not know that anyone interpreted the numbers as a call to violence. His lawyers have said that the slogan has long meant to “get rid of” or “eject” and has been featured on thousands of items sold online and regularly displayed at protests.
The Justice Department defends the James Comey prosecution in the Trump threat case. AP correspondent Mike Hempen has the latest.
But the department sought in its filings to place the post against the backdrop ofassassination plots or attemptsagainst Trump in the months before and after Comey’s post. Prosecutors say that two minutes before the post was made, Comey’s wife texted him a screenshot of a definition of “86” that said “to get rid of or refuse service.”
“There is no serious dispute that an objective viewer of Comey’s post could read it to mean ‘Kill President Trump,’” prosecutors wrote.
A portrait of President Donald Trump is displayed at the Justice Department building in Washington, June 2, 2026. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite, File)
The photo was posted days before Comey was set to release a novel he wrote titled “FDR Drive,” in which a prosecutor pursues a far-right social media personality who has called out his adversaries by name and inspired violence against them by his fans, the department said.
After the Instagram post provoked an outcry, according to the government’s filings, Comey’s publishing agent observed in a text message to him that he had “gone viral.” Comey responded that that was “not my intention, but I’ll be OK if it sells books.” The agent replied, ”Music to an agent’s ears.”
Prosecutors also asserted there was “reason to doubt” Comey’s account of having come upon the seashells while on a walk, saying they were located 4 miles (6 kilometers) “down from the beach from beachfront property where Comey was staying, in an area separated from the ocean by a sand dune.” They said there was “no evidence that anyone else arranged, photographed, or even saw the shells.”
Comey’s lawyers have called the indictment,which was filed months after an earlier and unrelated case against him was dismissed, part of a Trump retribution campaigntargeting one of the president’s vocal critics. Trumpfired Comey as head of the FBIin 2017 as Comey was overseeing an investigation into potential ties between Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and Russia. Trump since then has called for him and other perceived adversaries to be jailed.
But the Justice Department denied allegations of vindictiveness, saying the decision to indict Comey was made by the U.S. attorney in the area and did not stem from a directive from the president or the attorney general.
To bolster their claims that Comey was unjustly targeted, the defense team argued that investigators struggled to develop compelling evidence from witnesses that Comey had intended the post as a threat, but they concealed that from federal magistrates as they applied for warrants to search digital accounts associated with Comey and his wife
For instance, defense lawyers have said that the FBI searched an internal database of information about open and closed investigations for any indication of an association between Comey and the term “86” but found inconclusive results. An FBI agent also requested a review of the FBI file for the case against reputed mobster John Gambino, which Comey worked on as a young prosecutor, but found no references to the term “86.”
Investigators also interviewed a key government cooperator in the case, Salvatore “Sammy the Bull” Gravano, who said he did not recall ever discussing the term “86” with Comey or hearing it in connection with the trial.
The latest filings made clear that the administration was standing behind the premise of the case.
“No Government theory was disproved at that time, or now. No intentionally false omission exists, much less one made with reckless disregard for the truth,” prosecutors wrote.
“The evidence still supports that Defendant acted at least recklessly by consciously disregarding a substantial risk that his coded message of ‘8647’ that he sent to his 200,000 or so Instagram followers, and the millions of secondary social media users who would view this as threatening violence against the President of the United States,” they added.

item.title: 肯尼迪中心告诉法庭，不会在 9 月 8 日之前尝试恢复特朗普的名字
item.description:
华盛顿（美联社）——肯尼迪中心已向联邦法院表示，至少在 9 月 8 日之前，随着围绕该表演艺术场馆未来的另一场法律战即将展开，它不会试图将唐纳德·特朗普总统的名字重新印在大楼的正面。
在周二晚间提交的一份状态报告中，此举的反对者表示，肯尼迪中心与特朗普结盟的董事会成员“似乎有意”藐视早些时候法院要求将共和党总统的名字从大楼中删除的命令。肯尼迪中心表示，“最早”要到劳动节之后才会推进这些计划，以便有时间进行法律论证。
俄亥俄州民主党众议员乔伊斯·贝蒂 (Joyce Beatty) 是该委员会的当然成员，他的律师向美国地区法官克里斯托弗·库珀 (Christopher Cooper) 施压，要求其早日做出裁决，称“有充分理由相信，被告将在 9 月 8 日之后尽早尝试实施这项最新非法决议的部分或部分内容。”
本月举行的一次董事会会议原本预计将主要集中讨论关闭肯尼迪中心进行翻修的选择，但结果却变成了另一次推动将特朗普的名字贴在这座建筑上的努力，这是总统及其支持者在美国首都留下实体印记的海外行动的一部分。
董事会通过了一项决议，以特朗普的名字命名大楼前的广场，并将他的名字添加到场馆的正面，这样上面就会写着“由唐纳德·J·特朗普总统修复和翻新的约翰·F·肯尼迪表演艺术中心”。比蒂在文件中表示，如果特朗普肯尼迪中心基金达到 1 亿美元，董事会还同意增加对总统的额外提及。
在这种情况下，立面将写着“由唐纳德·J·特朗普总统修复和翻新的约翰·F·肯尼迪表演艺术中心，由特朗普·肯尼迪中心基金资助”。
董事会还投票支持关闭两年进行翻修，而该机构的一些标志性节目，包括肯尼迪中心荣誉奖和马克·吐温美国幽默奖，将在场外地点举行。国家交响乐团本周宣布，即将到来的演出季将在华盛顿及其周边的六个演出场地进行。
库珀五月裁定，贴在大楼上的写有特朗普名字的字母是非法添加的，他下令将其拆除，但政府未能说服法院推翻这一决定。从那时起，曾经安装这些字母的区域就被防水布覆盖了，这让那些试图从大楼上抹去总统名字的人感到沮丧。
在最新的文件中，肯尼迪中心没有承诺拆除防水布，称覆盖物的安装是为了方便删除特朗普的名字，并且是“对屋顶悬挑进行水测试和结构修复”所需的更广泛系统的一部分。
更广泛地说，比蒂的律师诺姆·艾森 (Norm Eisen) 和纳撒尼尔·泽林斯基 (Nathaniel Zelinsky) 对董事会本月投票的公正性提出了质疑，这与库珀在 3 月份呼吁关闭这座大楼的投票“信息不灵通且似乎是注定的”时提出的担忧相呼应。
在八月份的会议之前，肯尼迪中心的管理层表示，将向董事会提供三种选择，包括完全关闭或部分关闭，以允许“在不受工作影响的空间中继续进行一些公共访问和有限的活动”。第三种选择是“考虑一系列高度有限的分阶段关闭，以仅满足该中心最严重的基础设施需求，同时安排和维护全部项目。”
在周二的文件中，肯尼迪中心表示，达美咨询集团的一位分析师得出的结论是，部分关闭将在四年内完成，“将增加施工时间和成本，并导致严重的安全问题。”
肯尼迪中心表示，该分析师“建议董事会全面关闭两年，这将最大限度地降低总成本，最大限度地缩短节目因施工而受到干扰的时间，并最好地维护该中心作为世界级表演艺术场所的声誉。”
然而，艾森和泽林斯基指出，材料是在会议前两天才提供给董事会的。他们表示，一些文件似乎是在库珀 5 月裁决之前创建的，并提到肯尼迪中心的关闭最初定于 7 月 6 日生效。
比蒂的律师辩称，八月份关闭肯尼迪中心的投票“表现出了与第一次投票相同的缺陷”。

item.title: 民主党社会主义者安吉·尼克松周二在佛罗里达州赢得初选。她能在11月获胜吗？
item.description:
Florida Democratic voters delivered another shock upset to the party establishment by nominatingstate Rep. Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist,over Alex Vindman, a moderate former national security professional who played a central role in President Donald Trump’sfirst impeachment.
Democrats have hoped to mount a comeback in the diverse, populous and economically dynamic state but have struggled to craft a message that resonates in the Sunshine State’s political climate. Nixon’s upset sets up a long-shot challenge to U.S. Sen. Ashley Moody, a former state attorney general selected by Gov. Ron DeSantisto fill the seatafter Marco Rubio vacated it when Trump chose him as secretary of state.
The race has already inflamed tensions within the Democratic Party over how to energize liberal voters eager for unapologetic, combative candidates without alienating independents and moderates who have been key to winning in battleground states.
“If you’re surprised by tonight’s election results, you haven’t been paying enough attention to what’s happening in the South,” said Britney Whaley, the southeast regional director of the Working Families Party, which backs populist candidates. “Tonight’s election results must be a wake-up call to a political establishment that believes a populist message can’t win in the South. Angie’s campaign proves voters will respond to a bold economic vision that meets their basic needs.”
A spirited progressive who had the backing of Reps. Rashida Tlaib of Michigan and Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, Nixon is a longtime labor organizer who recently joined the Democratic Socialists of America. She championed policies like universal healthcare and childcare and has been an outspoken critic of U.S. foreign policy and the war in Gaza.
In May, Nixon protested the Republican-controlled Florida legislature’sredistricting of the state’s congressional mapsby shouting through a megaphone on the state House floor. She was later reprimanded by an ethics committee but earned plaudits from Democratic allies and voting rights groups for her demonstration.
Vindman raised about $16 million in his race and had spent more than $9 million by the end of July. Nixon, by contrast, had raised just shy of $1 million. Nixon eschewed broadcast television advertising, instead focusing on targeting voters on social media. She was backed by prominent online figures like children’s education influencer Ms. Rachel.
In contrast to other high-profile statewide democratic socialist bids this year, Nixon received little opposition from national Democratic figures or major political action committees. That didn’t stop progressives from immediately touting her win as a sign of greater momentum for the region.
Florida’s Senate race was widely considered out of reach for Democrats and not central to the party’s efforts to retake the upper chamber. Nevertheless, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin issued a statement praising Nixon as a “proven leader,” adding that the DNC “is ready to help elect Angie and work together to flip this seat.”
Vindman served on the White House’s National Security Council during Trump’s first term. His testimony was central to Trump’s first impeachment over a phone call in which the president pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to investigate Joe Biden and his family. Vindman became a national Democratic star and target of Trump’s ire for his actions, a dynamic that garnered him millions in small-dollar donations.
His twin brother Eugene, who also served on the council, is a Democratic congressman from Virginia.
“Rep. Nixon ran a strong campaign. I will be standing by her side in the fight against Ashley Moody. I hope you’ll join me,” Vindman said in a statement after he conceded the race.
Trump gleefully hailed Vindman’s defeat to Nixon.
“The most gratifying loss last night was that of a real treasonous creep, Alexander Vindman, to a Radical Left Lunatic, who can’t speak or think properly, and who will go down to certain defeat at the hands of Ashley Moody, a truly Fantastic Senator, from the Great State Florida,” Trump wrote on his social media platform, Truth Social. Trump added that Vindman “should be prosecuted for what he’d did!”
Democratic leaders like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer had hoped Vindman’s reputation and campaign war chest would turn what election analysts considered a solidly Republican seat into a more competitive race. Nixon’s upset victory has now buoyed already high Republican confidence in the state and raised progressive confidence about the strength of their message.
Vindman’s defeat mirrors that of others who rose to prominence opposing Trump during his first administration, when Democrats embraced “resistance” as a moniker for that opposition and for standing up for the rule of law. Their defeats may show how rank-and-file voters have shifted toward more strident and affirmative visions of politics.
In May, Rep. Al Green of Texas, a longtime Trump opponent and civil rights icon, lost a runoff race to Rep. Christian Menefee, a freshman progressive representative less than half Green’s age.
Rep. Dan Goldman, who served as counsel for House Democrats during Trump’s first impeachment, lost his primary in June to progressive challenger Brad Lander, who had the backing of New York City’s democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani. George Conway, a liberal lawyer who has garnered Trump’s ire, came in fifth place in another New York Democratic primary for U.S. House.
And earlier this month, Rep. Shri Thanedar of Michigan, who last year introduced articles of impeachment against Trump, lost his primary to a democratic socialist in a Detroit-area congressional race.
In multiple southern Florida congressional primaries Tuesday, left-flank candidates lost to more moderate ones. While the state has shifted rightward in recent election cycles, Florida has long been a refuge for Latino communities who had fled left-wing authoritarian regimes in Latin America. Many of those Floridians have consequently reacted negatively to anything or anyone labeled as socialist.
Elijah Manley, who finished third in a Broward County U.S. House primary won by Debbie Wasserman Schultz, acknowledged the tightrope. He got about 14% of the vote in a five-way race. In neighboring districts, Rep. Jared Moskowitz and political newcomer Pia Dandiya ran as moderates and won 64% and 69% of the vote, respectively, over more progressive opponents.
“I’m a proud moderate. We need more moderates,” Dandiya said in an interview.
The Senate returns showed similar trends. Nixon carried most of the state but was weakest in southern Florida, which includes some of the state’s largest Latino communities.
Still, Manley insisted the broader electorate wants a more aggressive, left-leaning party.
“They have looked at the Democratic establishment for the past four years, even 10 years, and it’s something that just isn’t working for them,” he said.
“Say what you will about the DSA. They’re organizing. They’re bringing people into the party. They’re exciting people, and they’re getting people. We should be happy that that’s happening,” Manley added.
Nixon’s allies view her voter base, which includes some of the most working-class and majority-Black counties in the state, as another path to power when coupled with the broader Democratic coalition. But they caution intraparty divisions and an inauthentic message could hamper a candidate from any wing of the party.
“I think people are looking for change. They’re looking for leadership who they can trust and who listens,” said Moné Holder, a liberal activist and urban planning committee chair who defeated a Republican for an at-large seat on Jacksonville’s city council.
“They’re looking for people to serve who aren’t wrapped up in political drama, but are about people. And I think voters came out to show that, and it proved itself in my election, and Angie’s, and a few others,” Holder said.
Associated Press writer Bill Barrow contributed to this report.

item.title: 副手试图在科罗拉多训练时向迪昂·桑德斯送达民事文件，但教练不在场
item.description:
上周，博尔德县治安官办公室的一名副手出现在科罗拉多大学校园，向迪昂·桑德斯送达民事文件，而当时教练正在公开训练，无法接近。
治安官办公室发言人周三表示，该警官被告知，布法罗队教练“当时无法收到文件收据”。据《今日美国》报道，桑德斯将被传唤作证，这是涉及他儿子希洛的破产审判的一部分，该审判将于 8 月 31 日开始。
科罗拉多州体育部门没有提供更多信息。水牛队将于 9 月 3 日在佐治亚理工学院拉开赛季序幕。
8月11日上午10点22分，这名副手带着民事文件抵达校园。那天，水牛队举行了公开训练，并制定了具体规则，观察到的任何情况都不能报告、发布或分享。
治安官办公室的高级通讯专家卡丽·哈弗菲尔德（Carrie Haverfield）在给美联社的电子邮件中写道，民事文件需要多次尝试送达的情况并不罕见。
哈弗菲尔德写道：“在与大学工作人员合作寻找更好的时间来完成这一过程时，我们从桑德斯先生的法律顾问那里得知，他们能够代表桑德斯先生收到文件收据，但是，他们不在博尔德县，所以我们将文件转移到丹佛进行送达。”“我们没有发现任何大学工作人员试图阻止公务员，相反，他们试图帮助我们的副手找到更好的时机这样做。我们不会透露我们所送达的民事文件的具体内容。”
希洛·桑德斯 (Shilo Sanders) 因高中时与保安发生的事件而引发的诉讼仍在诉讼中。该警卫对桑德斯提起诉讼，并因桑德斯缺席出庭而被判缺席判决。
去年八月，这位在科罗拉多为他父亲效力的强硬安全卫被坦帕湾海盗队裁掉。

item.title: 前温布尔登决赛选手尼克·克耶高斯因可卡因检测呈阳性而被停赛
item.description:
日内瓦（美联社）——前温布尔登决赛选手尼克·克耶高斯周三透露，他的可卡因检测呈阳性，并称兴奋剂案件给他敲响了警钟，因为伤病使他的职业生涯脱轨，他感到“无助和孤独”。
这位纪律记录不佳的31岁澳大利亚选手自2022年巅峰赛季以来仅在ATP巡回赛上打了10场单打比赛，只赢得了两场比赛，随后被暂时禁赛。随后，他进入了草地大满贯决赛，输给了诺瓦克·德约科维奇。
克耶高斯目前排名第919位。六月，他在西班牙一场低级别草地球场比赛中检测出派对毒品呈阳性。
“我最近在马略卡岛的一次药检中可卡因呈阳性，但未通过，”他在自己的 Instagram 账户上写道。“我犯了一个巨大的错误，并为此承担全部责任。”
这是这位才华横溢而又火热个性的职业生涯中最新的负面头条新闻，近年来他在球场上最引人注目的举动是去年 12 月在迪拜一场令人好奇的“性别之战”战胜阿丽娜·萨巴伦卡 (Aryna Sabalenka)。
克耶高斯面临长达四年的禁赛，但预计处罚会较轻。可卡因在比赛期间被禁止作为兴奋剂，而在比赛之外使用可卡因的处罚则较轻。
2017年的类似案件中，英国球员丹·埃文斯因在巴塞罗那公开赛上可卡因检测呈阳性而被国际网球联合会禁赛一年。
克耶高斯表示，在经历了两年的伤病之后，他很难接受职业生涯即将结束的事实。
“有时我感到无助和孤独。这些都不能成为我所做的事情的借口，”他说。他补充说，这些伤病“对我的身体和精神都造成了巨大的伤害。我的身体无法做到我的想法所期望的那样。”
克耶高斯今年单打战绩为1胜3负，上个月在温布尔登获得了双打外卡。他在第一轮中输给了搭档亚历山大·布布利克(Alexander Bublik)。
国际网球诚信机构将起诉此案，并表示该球员的样本于6月22日采集，并于7月17日在克耶高斯参加温网比赛后确认呈阳性。
ITIA 补充说，8 月 4 日实施了强制临时停职，克耶高斯并未提出上诉。
“然而，好消息是，这给我敲响了警钟，”克耶高斯写道，这表明他的职业生涯尚未结束。
“在接下来的 28 天里，我将远离社交媒体和公共生活，专注于让自己变得正确。”
克耶高斯职业生涯七个单打冠军中最近的一个是在温布尔登决赛后的第一场比赛中赢得的。2022 年 8 月，他在华盛顿特区举行的硬地赛事决赛中击败了西冈佳仁。
几周后，他进入美国公开赛四分之一决赛，输给了凯伦·卡恰诺夫。
2022 年 10 月在东京膝盖受伤后，克耶高斯在接下来的两年里只打了一次比赛，理由是手腕受伤错过了 2023 年温网。
克耶高斯在2025赛季的战绩仅为1胜4负，在澳网首轮比赛中失利，随后跳过了接下来的三项大满贯赛事。

item.title: 一名左截锋在大学橄榄球比赛中可以赚 400 万美元，但在 NFL 中则不然。这是付费玩吗？
item.description:
Left tackle Dan Moore of the Tennessee Titans can list all the sponsorship deals he has done as a pro on one hand: A few meet and greet opportunities when he was with the Steelers, a grill company that gave him some barbecue tools in exchange for his endorsement.
Million-dollar deals? No such thing, especially for someone playing his position. If he were in college — a talented offensive lineman with a chance to make his team a national contender — that might be different.
“It’s only been five years since NIL started,” said Moore, who heads into his sixth year in the NFL this season. “Another five years, and we could see college football becoming semi-pro.”
And that, in short, is the not-so-hidden secret driving anew era in college sports. It is a business rebuilt to allow players to cash in on theirname, image and likeness fame, one that pays exorbitant prices to athletes under the guise that the money isn’t a salary, but rather a payment for services the athletes provide through sponsorship deals.
That’s the way many of the headline-grabbing six- and seven-figure payments that go to college players for so-called“third party NIL”can truly comport with the NCAA rulebook. And that rulebook — for all its rapid changes in recent years — refuses to do away with the fading notion that college athletes aren’t pros who can be paid merely to show up and play.
Mike McGlinchey, a ninth-year NFL right tackle with the Denver Broncos, has a contract worth $52 million in guaranteed money but he doesn’t have a sponsorship deal. That puts him in the majority of NFL offensive linemen, who either don’t need to work extra for more income or aren’t well-known enough to grab much more than a local deal or two.
Of the 20 biggest NFL endorsement deals listed by Sportico – a list that starts with Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce at $32 million – not a single one belongs to a lineman.

But in college, there’s Jordan Seaton, the five-star left tackle who wasone of Deion Sanders’ biggest signingsat Colorado, then left the Buffs to play at LSU. There, in the heart of SEC country, Seaton reportedly makes $4 million for pitching a national chain pharmacy, a fast-food restaurant, a personal finance firm and others.
It’s a far cry from what McGlinchey envisioned when NIL arrived five years ago; he graduated from Notre Dame long before the era of paying college players began.
“What I thought NIL was supposed to mean was a local Ford dealership in South Bend puts the offensive line on a billboard and gives us a truck to drive around for six months,” he said. “Now, NIL means, ‘We have collectives of money and the one with the biggest checkbook is going to win.’ They’ve used name-image-likeness to open the floodgates to say. ‘We’re going to pay the most to get this kid.’”
Among the 20 highest-paid NFL endorsers are quarterbacks Geno Smith ($1.5 million), Sam Darnold ($1 million) and Deshaun Watson ($750,000).
All of those amounts are less than what the top 10 college players make in sponsorships, according to On3, which tracks college NIL deals, none of which are disclosed by schools. It’s a list that includes Seaton but does not include college football’s most widely recognizable name: Arch Manning, who reportedly took a pay cut this year to $2.5 million to help Texas beef up its roster.
Niklas Myhr, an associate professor at Chapman University and an expert in digital marketing, acknowledges the nod-nod, wink-wink element to all these NIL deals, but also thinks some of the numbers are the product of what he calls an “immature market.”
“Basically, there is no mature market for 20-year-old amateur athletes the way there is for sneakers,” he said. “So it’s basically reverse engineering a market.”
There is an agency in charge of enforcing the rules with the objective of putting guardrails around a spending spree exacerbated by atransfer portalthat encourages players to seek better offers from different schools.
Among the 14-month-oldCollege Sports Commission’stop missions is making sure companies partnered with schools — “associated entities” — are paying players an amount within a “fair range of compensation” compared to what others might receive for the same services. The CSC also verifies that those companies are using the athlete’s NIL for a “valid business purpose” — i.e., to promote goods and services provided to the general public for profit, as opposed to hanging onto, or “warehousing,” the NIL rights for future use or having the player simply show up to an event to shake hands.
“The valid business purpose, proper range of compensation evaluation is a key part of answering that question,” said Greg Sankey, the commissioner of the SEC, when asked if players were really being paid for anything beyond just showing up and playing. “And, in fact, it’s those who are signing those deals who need to answer those questions.”
Deals cut with non-associated entities — the definition of whichhas been disputed— aren’t subject to the same scrutiny. In theory, those deals, if truly between an athlete and a business with no connection to the school, are only limited by what the market will bear.
“I believe they’re arguing that coming to this high-profile college as a star player will warrant their NIL to become valuable just by brute force,” Myhr said, when asked how a brand justifies spending so much on a relatively unknown pitchman. “They believe they can predict the future value of this athlete is worth $1 million, or $4 million. That’s a stretch when it comes to transfering that (NIL) into captivating storytelling.”
While a good chunk of Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes’ $30 million in endorsements comes from his hard-to-miss State Farm TV commercials, it would be harder to spot most of college’s best-paid pitchmen.
Quarterback Darian Mensah’s featured NIL deal with Miami – histhird school in three years– is with a luxury watch company. Mensah’s NIL is believed worth $6.5 million, which is more than what all but nine current NFL players earn in endorsements, according to Sportico.
Among Seaton’s handful of NIL deals is one in which he goes on social media to tell his 77,000 Instagram followers of his love for Raising Cane’s — a chicken joint with roots in the Baton Rouge area that has strong connections to LSU. It helps explain how Seaton’s haul rose to about the same as that brought in by Livvy Dunne, the former LSU gymnast who has 5.1 million followers and is considered the highest female earner in the short history of third-party NIL.
Steve Denton, the CEO at Opendorse, which helps players find third-party NIL deals, argues the market is accurate because “college athletes have so much influence in their community that they actually perform better than influencers or creators.”
“Brands are clamoring to work with college athletes because sports is one of those things that slows people down and gets your attention,” Denton said.
Well aware of runaway costs of third-party NIL, college sports leaders are working in Washington on a solution that could address some of the transparency issues involved in NIL. A provision in theProtect College Sports Actawaiting a vote in the Senate would more than double the revenue-sharing amount schools can pay annually to athletes to nearly $49 million.
What’s different about that pool of money is that, because it’s not considered third-party NIL, it is excluded from scrutiny by the CSC. Under NCAA rules, that money couldn’t technically be considered a salary, but by removing it from the third-party NIL rules, it would do away with needing to justify the payments as legitimate NIL.
What would remain, according to industry leaders, would be a tranche of “organic” third-party NIL deals like Seaton’s agreement with Raising Cane’s. The deals presumably would not be related to any existing arrangement with multimedia rights (MMR) partners hired by the schools that currently broker deals with players.
Jon Bishop of Playfly Sports, an MMR company that looks to find deals for players and schools, sees the bill not so much imposing a cap on spending, but creating a new, and welcome lane for that organic NIL.
“There were certain brands ... that leaned in early, but many who set out thinking, ‘I don’t want be in the headlines because I paid someone on the side’ and all that stuff,” Bishop said. “So all of these things are just going to start to make a marketplace that actually will function, and I think function well.”
AP Sports Writer Teresa M. Walker in Nashville contributed to this story.

item.title: 债券市场的惊慌促使特朗普政府再次采取行动
item.description:
NEW YORK (AP) — Normally quiet, the bond market can occasionallysend warning signalsloud enough to hit stock markets worldwide and even grab the attention ofU.S. presidentsand other world leaders.
After the bond market’s alarm bells rose in volume through the summer, the Trump administration announced on Wednesday a move that could help calm it down. The U.S. Treasury Department said it will more than double the amount of U.S. government bonds that it will buy back, and the move worked in getting longer-term yields lower, for now at least.
Yields worldwide had earlier climbed to heights not reached in years and, in some cases, decades, because of the jump in oil prices due to thewar with Iran, worries aboutbig and growing debtsfor governments and other concerns.
The stakes are high because high yields drag on economies and bring downward pressure on stock markets after Wall Street hitrecordson excitement about big corporate profits and the promise ofartificial-intelligencetechnology.
But what’s to come is still uncertain, and some analysts warn the Treasury Department’s move could even ultimately backfire.
Here’s a look at what’s going on and how things got this way:
In the United States, the centerpiece of the bond market recently touched its highest yield in more than a year. The 10-year Treasury yield, which shows how much interest investors want the U.S. government to pay them before they’ll lend it money for a decade, topped 4.70%, before falling back to 4.65% Wednesday.
That’s up from just 3.97% before the Iran war began in late February, and it’s a significant move for the bond market.
More notably, the 30-year U.S. Treasury yield has jumped well above 5%, back to where it was in 2007, before the 2008 financial crisis sent yields crashing toward zero worldwide.
In Japan, the yield on the 10-year government bond has touched its highest level in nearly 30 years, while the German 10-year yield is back to where it was in 2011.
When the U.S. and other governments have to pay more in interest to borrow money, so do people and companies.
For many U.S. households, that’s most easily seen throughrates for mortgages. Such rates have climbed with the 10-year Treasury yield since the Iran war began, and the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage is near its highest level in a year.
Higher yields also make it more expensive for U.S. companies to borrow money to build factories and otherwise grow. That’s particularly dangerous at this moment, when big investments in data centers to power AI are amajor driver of the U.S. economy’s growth.
If high yields slow the economy, that puts pressure on the stocks. An economic slowdown would threaten how much profit companies can make, which is the lifeblood of the stock market.
High yields undercut the stock market in other ways too. When a Treasury is paying more in interest, that can draw investors away from investments that carry more risk. Why pay record prices for U.S. stocks when a U.S. government bond is paying more than before to wait in relative safety?
Gold, bitcoin and many other investments can also feel downward pressure from high yields.
When yields rise, the U.S. and other governments have to pay more in interest to cover their debts. That’s painful whendebt loads for governments worldwide are ballooningas they spend far more than they’re bringing in through revenue.
And if the U.S. government is already paying this much to borrow money when the economy is growing, what will happen if it needs to borrow even more to manage the pain when the next severe recession hits?
That’s why jumps in yields can scare politicians even more than swings in the stock market.
The bond market helped makeLiz Trussthe United Kingdom’s shortest-serving prime minister in 2022, whenit revolted against her planto cut taxes and raise spending without a way to pay for them.
Last year, President Donald Trump said thebond market may have played a rolein his decision to delay many of his proposed tariffs, saying that he noticed investors there “were getting a little queasy.”
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s move is a high-stakes effort to contain the rise in long-term yields, and some analysts are skeptical the impact will last.
“The operation changes almost nothing in terms of the fundamentals, in particular the unchanged need to finance the tidal wave of hyperscaler debt in addition to very large government deficits,” Krishna Guha, an analyst at Evercore ISI, and colleagues wrote in a note to clients.
“Hyperscalers” refers to the Big Tech companies that are borrowing mountains of money to build AI data centers. The bonds they’re selling are competing with U.S. Treasurys for buyers, which can push bond yields higher.
The U.S. government, meanwhile, continues to run its own large deficits regardless of what the Treasury Department does with its repurchases.
“The move could even backfire if the limited firepower results in little sustained impact,” Guha said.
The Federal Reserve could always cut the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term, overnight loans.
But longer-term yields like the 10- and 30-year Treasury yields are set by investors in the bond market. And recently, they have been demanding more in interest to make up for the growing risks of high inflation, continued government deficits and other factors.
The Fed also appears more likely to raise its benchmark short-term rate than to cut it. At its last meeting in late July, three Fed policymakersvoted to raise the fed funds rateseven as nine voted to keep it unchanged. And Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s decision to signal little about the Fed’s next moves appeared to push longer-term Treasury yields higher amid questions about what the central bank will do to get inflation back to its 2% target.
The government’s most recent inflation data suggest inflationmay be slowing, leading many on Wall Street to forecast the Fed will keep the federal funds rates steady at its next meeting in September. The next big potentially market-moving event may come on Aug. 28, when Warsh will give a speech at the Fed’s annual economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.

item.title: Moderna 表示其实验性 mRNA 癌症治疗通过了一项关键测试，股价飙升
item.description:
Moderna 周三宣布了一项实验性癌症治疗研究的初步结果，如果获得监管机构批准，该研究将是同类研究中的第一个，该公司股价周三上涨了一倍多。
Moderna 和默克公司正在开发一种基于 mRNA 的癌症疫苗 intismeran 的治疗方法，该疫苗旨在根据肿瘤内的独特突变为个体患者量身定制。在目前的研究中，他们将其与默克公司生产的免疫治疗药物 Keytruda 配对。
该研究比较了黑色素瘤患者同时使用 intismeran 和 Keytruda 与单独使用 Keytruda 的情况。两家公司表示，与单独使用 Keytruda 的患者相比，接受该组合治疗的患者在没有癌症复发或转移的情况下寿命更长。
两家公司没有透露患者在癌症不复发的情况下存活了多长时间，也没有透露患者的总体寿命是否更长。他们表示计划在即将召开的国际医学会议上展示研究结果。
Moderna 股价上涨超过 120%，至每股 140.12 美元。默克公司股价上涨约11%。

item.title: 特朗普表示美国和加拿大已达成贸易协议，但关键条款仍不清楚
item.description:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Canada and the United States moved closer Wednesday tofinalizing a trade agreementthat would avert threatened 50% U.S. tariffs, with a senior Canadian official calling the emerging terms “a very good deal for Canada” while cautioning that negotiations were not complete.
President Donald Trump said the agreement was “very fair” to both sides and predicted U.S. farmers and manufacturers would benefit. The tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian imports have been postponed until 12:01 a.m. Saturday.
The senior Canadian official said the emerging agreement would provide greater certainty, protect Canada’s dairy sector and jobs threatened by the new tariffs, and preserve what Ottawa considers favorable trade terms with the United States.
Prime Minister Mark Carney asked provincial premiers during a briefing to return U.S. alcohol to store shelves, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said, a step aimed at addressing one of the Trump administration’s key trade complaints. Houston and two other premiers voiced support for the direction of the talks, though Houston said whether Canadians would actually buy U.S. alcohol again “is a whole other discussion.”
The senior official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the negotiations publicly before an agreement is finalized.
Last month, Trump invoked a never-before-used legal authority, dating back to the Great Depression, to announce that the United States would slap 50% tariffs on $20 billion, or about 5%, of Canadian exports to the United States, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors.
Trump claimed that Canada discriminates against American exports of autos, alcohol and cheese. The U.S. president is also furious that Canada and China were the only countries that punched back with retaliatory tariffs of their own when he slapped levies on their products.
While details of the agreement emerging Wednesday remain vague, Trump claimed Canada had agreed to end tariffs on U.S. agricultural products. “The tariffs will be non-existent for our farmers. Our farmers were paying tremendous tariffs into Canada, and those tariffs are going to be totally eviscerated. Down to zero,” he said.
Canada currently allows a set amount of dairy imports at low tariffs. Once imports exceed that limit, much higher tariffs apply. The U.S. says Canada’s “supply management″ system makes it harder for American dairy producers to get full access to the Canadian market.
Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-U.S. trade, told reporters in Washington that Canada’s “agriculture sector will be well protected and we have maintained our tough line.”
The senior Canadian official was even more explicit, saying supply management was “not on the table” and Canada’s dairy system would remain protected.
That leaves another key question unresolved: how Canada can preserve supply management while giving U.S. farmers the additional access Trump says they will get.
Canada has not publicly detailed what tariff relief Washington has offered.
But the senior Canadian official said the emerging agreement would avert the new 50% tariffs, protect a significant number of jobs and preserve Canada’s favorable access to the U.S. market.
The official also said the agreement would allow Canada to focus more on its domestic economic agenda, including infrastructure projects, attracting foreign investment and diversifying exports beyond the United States.
Provincial leaders also signaled that a trade agreement would not mean returning to the previous Canada-U.S. economic relationship. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said “the old status quo is not possible,” while British Columbia Premier David Eby said, agreement or not, “we will not go back to the way things were before.”
In announcing the tariff pause, Trump said the long-canceled Keystone XL pipeline “may be awoken from the grave,” though he did not say it was part of the agreement. The project, designed to carry Canadian crude to U.S. refineries, was rejected by Barack Obama, revived by Trump and canceled again by Joe Biden.
Carney had already raised reviving Keystone XL with Trump at the White House in October 2025, and Trump was receptive, according to a Canadian government official familiar with the discussion. A revival would align with a longstanding Canadian goal rather than amount to a new U.S. concession.
Eight of Canada’s 10 provinces restrict or ban U.S. alcohol — measures imposed in retaliation for Trump’s previous tariffs on a number of Canadian goods last year and amid anger over his repeated talk of making Canada the 51st U.S. state. The Distilled Spirits Council says U.S. spirits exports to Canada have fallen more than 70%.
Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, is especially important. Its government-run LCBO, one of the world’s largest alcohol purchasers, sold nearly $1 billion Canadian dollars ($723 million) in U.S. products annually before pulling them from shelves.
The White House says the emerging deal includes a Canadian commitment to address the restrictions. But Carney cannot order provinces to restore sales.
The backlash extends beyond liquor stores, with Canadian travel to the United States falling sharply. Even if U.S. alcohol returns, sales could take time to recover.
The U.S. isrenegotiating a North American trade pact— the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement — that Trump strong-armed America’s neighbors into accepting in his first term. The U.S. has begun formal USMCA negotiations with Mexico but not with Canada.
The senior Canadian official said resolving the immediate tariff dispute would provide a path toward broader USMCA negotiations.
If the threat of 50% tariffs is cleared, it “should help pave the way for formal U.S.-Canada negotiations,’' said Wendy Cutler, a former U.S. trade negotiator who is now senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
Both countries had incentives to head off an escalation in trade tensions.
Nearly 72% of Canada’s goods exports last year went to the United States. And the Trump administration might be wary of imposing a hefty new tariff — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — ahead of November’s midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
